title: Heaps & priority queues, tree traversals
summary: A binary min-heap stores a priority queue in an array so that add and removeSmallest are Θ(log N). Final questions trace swim/sink on arrays, check or build heaps (bottom-up heapify), use PQs for top-k and median problems, and test the four tree traversals, including rebuilding a tree from two traversals.

lesson.title: Priority queues and the heap shape

blocks.text: Supports add(x), getSmallest(), removeSmallest(), size(). Only the minimum is ever requested, so a fully sorted structure is overkill.

A binary tree that is (1) complete — every level full except possibly the last, filled left to right — and (2) heap-ordered — every node ≤ each of its children. The minimum is the root. Siblings are unordered.
Because the tree is complete, store it in an array level by level. With the root at index 1 (index 0 unused):
With the root at index 0 instead: children 2k + 1 and 2k + 2, parent (k − 1) / 2.

blocks.title: Check the heap property
steps: Check every k ≥ 2: a[k/2] ≤ a[k].
(b) index 5 holds 1, parent index 2 holds 4 > 1: invalid.
(d) any sorted array is a heap: valid.

blocks.title: Where can each rank live?
blocks.prompt: In a min-heap of the 7 distinct keys 1…7, which array indices can hold key 2, key 3, and key 7?
steps: Key 2 must be a child of the root: every ancestor must be smaller, and only 1 is smaller. Indices 2 or 3.
Key 3 has at most two smaller keys, so its depth is ≤ 2: indices 2–7 (any non-root position).
Key 7 (the maximum) can have no children (both would need to be larger): it must be a leaf, indices 4–7.
A brute force over all 5040 orderings finds 80 valid heaps and confirms these position sets.

blocks.title: Insert trace
blocks.prompt: Add 6, 2, 9, 1, 5, 3, 8, 0 to an empty min-heap. Give the array after each add.
steps: 6: [6]. 2: goes to index 2, parent 6 > 2 → swap: [2, 6]. 9: [2, 6, 9].
1: index 4, parent (index 2) 6 → swap → index 2, parent 2 → swap: [1, 2, 9, 6].
3: index 6, parent (index 3) 9 → swap; parent 1 stops: [1, 2, 3, 6, 5, 9].
0: index 8, swaps with 6 (index 4), 2 (index 2), 1 (index 1): [0, 1, 3, 2, 5, 9, 8, 6].

blocks.title: removeSmallest trace
steps: Remove 0: last item 6 to the root: [6, 1, 3, 2, 5, 9, 8]. Sink: smaller child 1 → swap; at index 2 children 2, 5 → swap with 2: [1, 2, 3, 6, 5, 9, 8].
Remove 1: 8 to root: [8, 2, 3, 6, 5, 9]. Smaller child 2 → swap; at index 2 children 6, 5 → swap with 5: [2, 5, 3, 6, 8, 9].
Remove 2: 9 to root: [9, 5, 3, 6, 8]. Smaller child 3 → swap; index 3 has no children: [3, 5, 9, 6, 8].

blocks.text: Sink swaps with the smaller child. Swapping with the left (or larger) child can put a larger key above a smaller one. And a heap is not sorted: the maximum is somewhere among the leaves (second half of the array), so finding it is Θ(N).

Given N items in an array, inserting them one by one costs O(N log N). Bottom-up heapify is faster: sink every non-leaf, from index N/2 down to 1. Each sink fixes a subtree whose children are already heaps.

blocks.name: Bottom-up heapify is Θ(N)
blocks.text: A node at height h sinks at most h levels; there are about N/2^(h+1) nodes of height h, so total work ≤ Σ h·N/2^(h+1) = O(N).

proof.text: Measured on reverse-sorted input: bottom-up heapify used 1015 swaps for N = 1024 and 262,127 for N = 262,144 (≈ N), while inserting one at a time used 8204 and 4,194,324 (≈ N log N / 2).

blocks.title: Heapify trace
blocks.prompt: Heapify [9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2, 6, 3, 5] (index 1 first, N = 9). Show the array after each sink.
steps: Non-leaves are indices 4, 3, 2, 1.
sink(4): key 1, children 3 and 5 are larger: no change.
sink(3): key 7, children 2 and 6 → swap with 2: [9, 4, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6, 3, 5].
sink(2): key 4, children 1 and 8 → swap with 1 (index 4); then children 3 and 5 → swap with 3: [9, 1, 2, 3, 8, 7, 6, 4, 5].
sink(1): key 9, children 1 and 2 → swap with 1; at index 2 children 3, 8 → swap with 3; at index 4 children 4, 5 → swap with 4: [1, 3, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6, 9, 5].

head: Operation
Binary heap
rows: Θ(log N) (amortized if the array resizes)

blocks.title: Top k largest of a stream
blocks.prompt: Keep the k largest of N items using Θ(k) memory. Trace k = 3 on 5, 1, 9, 3, 7, 9, 2, 8.
steps: Use a min-heap of size ≤ k: add each item; if size exceeds k, removeSmallest. The heap always holds the k largest seen so far and its min is the k-th largest.
Cost: Θ(N log k) time, Θ(k) space — better than sorting (Θ(N log N), Θ(N) space).

blocks.title: Running median with two heaps
blocks.prompt: Maintain the median of a stream: max-heap lo (smaller half) and min-heap hi (larger half), with |lo| = |hi| or |lo| = |hi| + 1. Trace 5, 15, 1, 3, 8, 7, 9, 10, reporting lo’s max (the lower median) after each.
steps: add x: if lo is empty or x ≤ lo.max, add to lo, else to hi. Rebalance: if |lo| > |hi| + 1 move lo.max to hi; if |hi| > |lo| move hi.min to lo.
Each add is Θ(log N), median query Θ(1).

blocks.text: Other PQ uses: Dijkstra/Prim (next closest vertex), merging k sorted lists (heap of k list heads, Θ(N log k)), event simulation, heapsort.
Visit node, then left subtree, then right subtree.
Left, node, right. On a BST this lists keys in sorted order.
Left, right, node. Children are finished before their parent (e.g. computing sizes, deleting a tree).
Depth 0, then depth 1, … left to right; use a queue (BFS).

blocks.title: All four traversals
blocks.prompt: Tree: 8(3(1, 6(4, 7)), 10(·, 14(13, ·))). Give pre-, in-, post- and level-order.
steps: Preorder: 8, then left subtree 3, 1, 6, 4, 7, then right 10, 14, 13.
Inorder: 1 3 4 6 7 8 10 13 14 (sorted: it is a BST).
Postorder: 1 4 7 6 3, then 13 14 10, then 8.

blocks.text: Iterative preorder: a stack; pop and visit, then push right child before left child (so left is processed first). Replacing the stack with a queue gives level order.

blocks.title: Rebuild a tree from preorder + inorder
blocks.prompt: Preorder 5 2 1 4 3 8 6 9, inorder 1 2 3 4 5 6 8 9. Rebuild the tree and give its postorder.
steps: The first preorder item, 5, is the root. In the inorder, 5 splits {1 2 3 4} (left) from {6 8 9} (right).
Left part: next preorder item 2 is its root; inorder splits {1} and {3 4}. 1 is a leaf. In {3 4}, the next preorder item 4 is the root, and 3 is its left child.
Right part: preorder continues 8: root; inorder {6} left, {9} right.

blocks.title: Rebuild from postorder + inorder
steps: The last postorder item, 1, is the root: inorder left {3 2 5 4}, right {6 8 7 9}.
Work backward through the postorder, building the right subtree first: 6 is the right part’s root; inorder: nothing left of 6, {8 7 9} right; 7 is that root with 8 left, 9 right.
Left part {3 2 5 4}: next (backward) is 2: left {3}, right {5 4}; 4 is root of {5 4} with 5 on its left.

blocks.text: Preorder + postorder alone don’t determine a binary tree: 1 with only a left child 2 and 1 with only a right child 2 both have preorder 1 2 and postorder 2 1. You need inorder (or extra information such as “it is a BST” or “it is full”).

cards.front: Two properties of a binary min-heap?

back.text: Complete shape (levels full, last filled left to right) and heap order (each node ≤ its children).

cards.front: Array index formulas (root at 1)?

back.text: parent k/2, left 2k, right 2k + 1.

cards.front: Array index formulas (root at 0)?

back.text: parent (k − 1)/2, children 2k + 1 and 2k + 2.

cards.front: add in a heap?

back.text: Put the item at the end (index n + 1) and swim: swap with parent while smaller. Θ(log N).

cards.front: removeSmallest in a heap?

back.text: Save the root, move the last item to the root, shrink, sink: swap with the smaller child while larger. Θ(log N).

cards.front: Why sink with the smaller child?

back.text: The smaller child becomes the parent of the other, so heap order holds.

cards.front: Where is the maximum in a min-heap?

back.text: At some leaf (indices n/2 + 1 … n). Finding it is Θ(N).

cards.front: Is a sorted array a valid min-heap?

back.text: Yes.

cards.front: Bottom-up heapify and its cost?

back.text: Sink indices n/2 down to 1; Θ(N) total.

cards.front: Cost of building a heap by N inserts?

back.text: O(N log N) (Θ(N log N) worst case, e.g. decreasing input).

cards.front: Positions of the 2nd smallest key in a min-heap?

back.text: A child of the root (index 2 or 3).

cards.front: Can a tree with ≥ 2 nodes be both a min-heap and a BST?

back.text: No: the root’s left child must be both larger (heap) and smaller (BST); completeness forces a left child.

cards.front: Convert a BST into a min-heap in Θ(N)?

back.text: Inorder traversal produces a sorted array, which is a min-heap.

cards.front: Top-k largest with a PQ?

back.text: Min-heap of size k: add, and remove the min when size exceeds k. Θ(N log k) time, Θ(k) space.

cards.front: Running median data structure?

back.text: Max-heap of the lower half + min-heap of the upper half, sizes within 1.

cards.front: Merge k sorted lists of total N items?

back.text: Min-heap of the k current heads: Θ(N log k).

cards.front: Preorder / inorder / postorder definitions?

back.text: Node-L-R / L-node-R / L-R-node.

cards.front: What does inorder give on a BST?

back.text: Keys in sorted order.

cards.front: Level-order traversal uses which structure?

back.text: A queue (it is BFS on the tree).

cards.front: Which traversal pairs determine a binary tree with distinct keys?

back.text: Inorder plus preorder, or inorder plus postorder. Preorder + postorder does not (unless the tree is full).

cards.front: Rebuild from preorder + inorder: the method?

back.text: First preorder item is the root; split the inorder at it; recurse on the left part then the right part, consuming preorder items in order.

cards.front: Iterative preorder?

back.text: Stack: pop, visit, push right child, then left child.

cards.front: Θ of removing the k smallest items from a heap of N?

back.text: Θ(k log N).

hard.title: k-th smallest of a heap without destroying it

prompt.text: Given a min-heap array h[1..n] (do not modify it), find the k-th smallest key in O(k log k) time. Find the 1st, 4th and 7th smallest of h = [1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 9, 7, 8, 10].

hard.answer: Expand a frontier with an auxiliary min-PQ of indices; answers 1, 4, 7

solution.text: Idea: the smallest key is h[1]; the next smallest is always a child of some already-extracted node. Keep an auxiliary min-PQ of candidate indices ordered by h[index].
Each step removes one candidate and adds at most two, so the auxiliary PQ holds ≤ k + 1 entries: O(k log k), independent of n.
On the example: 1st = 1, 4th = 4, 7th = 7 (verified).

hard.title: Median priority queue

prompt.text: Design a structure with add(x) in O(log N), getMedian() in Θ(1) (lower median when N is even), and removeMedian() in O(log N). State the invariants and write add.

hard.answer: Max-heap lo + min-heap hi, every lo ≤ every hi, |lo| − |hi| ∈ {0, 1}; median = lo.max

solution.text: Invariants: (1) every key in lo ≤ every key in hi; (2) |lo| = |hi| or |lo| = |hi| + 1. Then lo.max is the lower median.
Each operation does O(1) heap operations: O(log N). Trace on 5, 15, 1, 3, 8, 7, 9, 10 gives medians 5 5 5 3 5 5 7 7 and ends with lo = {1, 3, 5, 7}, hi = {8, 9, 10, 15} (verified).

hard.title: Remove the k smallest into a balanced BST

prompt.text: Given a min-heap of N distinct keys and k ≤ N, build a perfectly balanced BST containing the k smallest keys. Give an algorithm and its runtime.

hard.answer: removeSmallest k times into an array (sorted), then build the BST from the middle recursively: Θ(k log N)

solution.text: k calls to removeSmallest produce the k smallest in increasing order: Θ(k log N).
From a sorted array a[lo..hi], the balanced BST has root a[mid], left subtree from a[lo..mid−1], right from a[mid+1..hi]: Θ(k).
Total Θ(k log N). (If the heap must survive, use the k-th smallest frontier technique to read them in O(k log k) instead.)

prompt.text: For reverse-sorted input of size N, compare the number of swaps for (a) bottom-up heapify and (b) inserting the items one at a time into an empty min-heap. Give Θ for each and explain (b).

solution.text: (a) Heapify sinks each non-leaf at most its height; Σ heights = O(N). Measured: 1015 swaps for N = 1024, 16,371 for 16,384, 262,127 for 262,144.

(b) Each new item is smaller than everything present, so it swims all the way to the root: ⌊log₂ i⌋ swaps for the i-th insert, and Σ log i = Θ(N log N). Measured: 8204, 196,624 and 4,194,324 swaps for N = 2¹⁰, 2¹⁴, 2¹⁸, which is almost exactly N(log₂ N − 2).

prompt.text: A general tree is stored with class S { int v; S child, sib; } (child = first child, sib = next sibling). Write recursive size(t), height(t) (edges; a lone node has height 0) and maxDegree(t). For the tree 1 → {2, 3, 4}, 2 → {5, 6}, 4 → {7}, 7 → {8}, give all three.

solution.text: Key insight: in this representation the sib pointer leads to nodes at the same depth, so height adds 1 only along child. Call each on the root (whose sib is null).
Results: size 8, height 3 (1 → 4 → 7 → 8), max degree 3 (node 1). Verified.

prompt.text: A min-heap holds the distinct keys 1 … 15 in a complete tree of height 3 (array indices 1 … 15). (a) Which indices can hold key 15? (b) What is the largest key that can be at index 2? (c) What is the smallest key that can be at index 15?

solution.text: (a) The maximum must be a leaf: indices 8 … 15.

(b) Index 2’s subtree has 7 nodes (indices 2, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11), all ≥ h[2]. So at least 6 keys exceed h[2]: h[2] ≤ 15 − 6 = 9. Achievable: put 1 at the root, 2 … 8 in the right subtree (index 3’s 7 positions), and 9 … 15 in the left subtree with 9 at index 2.
(c) Index 15’s ancestors are indices 7, 3, 1, all smaller: h[15] ≥ 4. Achievable with h[1] = 1, h[3] = 2, h[7] = 3, h[15] = 4 and the rest filled validly.

hard.title: Iterate a MinPQ using only its interface

prompt.text: Given a MinPQ<T> with only add, removeSmallest, getSmallest, size, write an Iterator<T> that yields items in increasing order but leaves the original PQ unchanged when iteration finishes. Give the cost of a full iteration.

hard.answer: Copy into an auxiliary PQ at construction (or drain into a list and re-add); Θ(N log N)

solution.text: Constructor: repeatedly removeSmallest from the PQ into a list (sorted, Θ(N log N)), then add each back to the PQ (Θ(N log N)). Keep an index into the list.
hasNext: index < list.size(). next: list.get(index++).
Total Θ(N log N); the PQ ends with the same items (its internal arrangement may differ, which the interface can’t observe).

hard.title: Rebuild a BST from preorder alone

prompt.text: Show that the preorder of a BST with distinct keys determines the tree, and write an O(N) rebuild. Rebuild from 10 5 1 7 40 50.

solution.text: The inorder of a BST is the sorted keys, so preorder + sorted order already determine it. Faster: pass bounds.
Each key is consumed once and each failed bound check returns immediately: O(N). Result 10(5(1, 7), 40(·, 50)) (verified).

keyFacts: Min-heap = complete tree + each node ≤ its children; array with root at 1: parent k/2, children 2k, 2k + 1.
add: append + swim; removeSmallest: last to root + sink with the smaller child; both Θ(log N); getSmallest Θ(1).
Bottom-up heapify (sink n/2 … 1) is Θ(N); N inserts is Θ(N log N) worst.
Max of a min-heap is a leaf; heaps are not sorted; search is Θ(N).
Top-k: size-k min-heap, Θ(N log k). Median: max-heap + min-heap, sizes within 1.
Pre = node L R; in = L node R (sorted for a BST); post = L R node; level order = queue.
Inorder + (pre or post) determines a binary tree; pre + post does not.

parsons.goal: Min-heap in h[1..n]. Move the item at index k down, always swapping with the smaller child, until heap order holds.
